title: Iron Deficiency in Plants: Signs, Causes and How to Fix It
metaTitle: Iron Deficiency in Plants: Signs and Fixes
metaDescription: Iron deficiency shows on the young leaves first. See the signs crop by crop, what causes it, and the fertilizer sold here that fixes it.
excerpt: Iron deficiency in plants starts on the young leaves and the growing tip. Iron is needed to make and keep chlorophyll, so without it new leaves cannot turn green. It is part of the enzymes that run photosynthesis and respiration. It also helps the plant use nitrate and sulfate to build proteins. Here are the signs in each crop, what brings it, how to be sure and the fertilizer that fixes it.

heroImage.alt: Gardenia twig with young leaves yellow between dark green veins from iron shortage

blocks.text: Iron does not move out of old leaves, so the yellowing shows on the newest leaves first. In bad cases the youngest leaves turn almost white while the old ones stay green.
Iron deficiency symptoms

Young leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, a pattern that runs the full length of the leaf. As it worsens, the whole leaf turns pale yellow to white, and the leaf edges may scorch brown. Growth slows and yield drops, and in rice a severe case can kill the plant. It is worst on limy, compacted or waterlogged ground.

Each crop shows it its own way. So find yours in the tables below, then open its page for the photo and the full fix, like the one for [iron in rice](/nutrient-deficiencies/rice-nutrient-deficiency#iron).

blocks.text: What causes iron deficiency

Iron shortage comes mostly on calcareous, alkaline or over limed soils, where high pH turns iron into forms roots cannot take. Upland crops on neutral to alkaline soils, fields irrigated with alkaline water, and soils low in organic matter are most at risk. Wet, compacted soils and very high phosphorus make it worse. On acid, flooded rice soils the problem is usually the opposite, with too much iron.
How to be sure it is iron

Manganese shortage also yellows young leaves between the veins. But as small yellow spots, while iron chlorosis is smooth and turns leaves whitish. Zinc makes pale bands near the leaf base, and in flooded rice, sulfide damage looks like iron shortage but blackens the roots. Check the soil pH first, because iron shortage usually comes with high pH or too much lime. A DA Regional Soils Laboratory can test soil iron, and a leaf tissue test helps. A trial spray of iron on a few plants is a quick check, because the new leaves green up within days if iron was short.
How to fix iron deficiency

On high pH soils most iron products fail in the soil. Only an iron chelate called FeEDDHA works well above pH 7.2. For fruit trees, a mix of ferrous sulfate and elemental sulfur placed in holes around the drip line lowers the pH near the roots. Use ammonium sulfate instead of urea, and add compost or manure.

A typical spray is about 0.5 percent ferrous sulfate (5 grams per liter) or an iron chelate by its label, and it works within days. The green fades as new leaves grow, so repeat the spray, and spray in the evening to avoid leaf burn.

How to keep iron deficiency away
Do not over lime, and on calcareous soils choose iron efficient varieties and acidifying fertilizers such as ammonium sulfate. Keep organic matter up, and avoid waterlogging and heavy phosphorus.

blocks.title: Too much is a problem too
blocks.text: In flooded, acid rice soils, too much iron is the more common problem, reported in many Central Luzon rice areas. Iron toxicity starts as tiny brown spots at the tips of the lower leaves, which spread until the leaves turn orange to brown.

blocks.text: Iron deficiency questions

items.q: What does iron deficiency look like?
items.a: The newest leaves turn yellow between green veins, and in bad cases the whole young leaf turns almost white. The old leaves stay green.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for iron deficiency?
items.a: On high pH soil, a foliar spray of ferrous sulfate or an iron chelate gives the quickest result. For the soil, only an iron chelate made for alkaline soil (FeEDDHA) works well above pH 7.2.

items.q: Why are the young leaves of my plants yellow but the old ones green?
items.a: Shortages of iron, zinc, manganese, sulfur or calcium all start on young leaves, because these nutrients do not move out of old leaves. Iron is the likely one if the soil is limy and the yellow lies between green veins.

items.q: How often should I spray iron?
items.a: Spray again whenever new pale leaves appear, because the green from one spray does not carry over to new growth. Spray in the evening or on a cool, cloudy day to avoid leaf burn.
